extracted.intended_audience: university administrators, deans, program managers, and faculty responsible for financial decisions about online courses and programs
extracted.subtask_short: making financial decisions for online programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for deciding about offering, pricing, continuing, or replacing components of online course offerings (courses, programs, production units, capital equipment) using CVP, relevant costing, discounted cash flow, and activity-based costing techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution margin / CVP arithmetic (measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total Revenue (units × price) less Total Variable Costs (units × variable cost per unit) equals Total Contribution Margin; less Total Fixed Costs equals Net Revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter shows the contribution-margin income statement format and applies it to per-student and total calculations for courses (Tables 1–2). Use contribution margin format to determine how additional units (students) change net revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: CVP analysis assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: CVP analysis assumes that: (1) total costs can be divided into fixed and variable components; (2) behaviour of total revenues and total costs is linear in relation to units of output within the relevant range; (3) selling price and variable costs per unit are known; (4) time value of money is ignored (can be relaxed later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions must hold (or be reasonably approximated) for break-even and contribution margin calculations to be valid. The text warns about range limits (e.g., bulk discounts) and later reintroduces time value of money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break-even in units formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Break-even in units = Total Fixed Costs / Per-unit Contribution Margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute minimum students required to cover fixed instructor costs (e.g., Course A: $3,000/($300–100) = 15). Apply per-activity fixed costs (direct fixed) when determining break-even for that activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contribution margin per unit to choose among alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If a decision-maker is indifferent between alternatives, recommend the option with higher contribution margin per additional unit, assuming fixed costs do not change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Course A contributes $200/student vs Course B $100/student; directing an indifferent student to Course A increases net revenue by $200 vs $100. Watch for the point where added volume triggers hiring (fixed cost increases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment margin analysis (direct vs indirect fixed costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment margin analysis separates fixed costs into direct (course-specific, disappear if discontinued) and indirect (central administration salaries, etc.) to compute segment margin = Contribution Margin – Direct Fixed Costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When indirect fixed costs are appropriately segregated, the registration level required to cover direct fixed costs can be significantly lower; decisions to cancel should consider segment margin (e.g., Course B's positive segment margin of $900 means it should not be cancelled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant costs — three criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant costs for a decision must: (1) differ between alternatives; (2) be future costs (not sunk); (3) involve cash outlays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all three tests: allocated indirect fixed costs that do not change between alternatives are irrelevant (example: allocated admin salaries). The chapter uses examples (document management, one-time contracts) to illustrate the threefold test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunk costs are irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Past costs that have already been incurred (sunk costs) should not influence current or future decisions because they cannot be changed by current actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: even if project costs to date exceed initial estimates, decision at year‑2 should be based on future incremental costs and benefits. Cancelling based on sunk costs would increase loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only cash outlays are relevant; amortization is non-cash
rubrics_metrics.description: Amortization and other paper allocations do not involve cash outlays and should be excluded when determining relevant cash flows for decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: capital grant and amortization were obscuring true cash flows in an online program; restating to show actual cash outflows/inflows (recording computer purchase as Year 1 cash outflow, excluding amortization) revealed the program produced net cash inflows in Years 2–5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental (marginal) analysis for one-time offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate one-time contracts or special offers by considering only incremental revenues and the variable/future costs that will change as a result; allocated fixed costs that do not change are irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: producing six courses at $19,000 each appears to lose money if using average cost per course, but when irrelevant allocated fixed costs are removed, incremental analysis showed a positive contribution of $57,000, so the offer should be accepted if no additional fixed costs are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed costs can be relevant if incurred as a result of the decision
rubrics_metrics.description: A previously fixed cost becomes relevant when the decision will cause an additional fixed cash outlay (e.g., needing an extra $40,000 platform cost to produce additional courses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include such incremental fixed costs in the incremental analysis (example: $57,000 contribution – $40,000 new fixed cost = $17,000 incremental net revenue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity constraints: maximize contribution margin per unit of scarce resource
rubrics_metrics.description: When operating at capacity, choose the alternative that yields the highest contribution margin per unit of the scarce resource (e.g., contribution margin per person-hour), not simply per unit of product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Faculty of Arts contributed $10,000 per course but took 1,000 hours (giving $10 per hour) versus Faculty of Medicine $30,000 but 4,000 hours ($7.50 per hour); under a 40-person-hour/day constraint, the Arts courses are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital asset replacement decision criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignore original purchase price (sunk); consider purchase price of new asset, expected sale (salvage) of old asset, future maintenance/operating cost differences, production savings, and estimated useful life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a one-day-old copier (sunk $20,000) vs new copier for $25,000 that saves $.03/page; include sale of old machine and production savings to compute net cost savings ($7,000) and decide to purchase the new machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time value of money: PV/FV and annuity formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Future value: F = P(1 + r)^n. Present value: P = F/(1 + r)^n. Present value of an equal-payment series: P = F[1 - (1 + r)^-n]/r. Present value equivalent lump-sum formula also provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables (Appendices) or formulas to convert future cash flows to present values when cash inflows/outflows occur at different times (examples compute PV of $100 in 2 years at 10% = $82.60; annuity and lump-sum equivalences shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) analysis for decisions and capital budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine relevant future cash flows with the time value of money to translate future inflows/outflows to present value and assess investment alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: purchase of new equipment costing $24,000 with $6,000/year savings over 4 years; discount savings and salvage at the required rate (10% or 20%) to compute discounted net cost savings and decide whether to replace equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity-based costing / time-driven ABC (TDABC) for pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate all resources needed to produce a product/service: (1) identify direct costs (only to the point worth the effort); (2) combine indirect costs into cost pools of similar activities; (3) identify a cost-allocation basis related to cost incurrence for each pool; (4) calculate appropriate hourly/application rates using realistic allocation bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter walks through creating Administration, Building, and Insurance cost pools, selecting allocation bases (manager hours, project-days, projects per year), and calculating application rates (e.g., $80/hr admin, $2/day building, $50/project insurance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate quoted price using application rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine programmer/manager estimated hours, application rates for indirect pools, days active, and fixed per-project costs to produce a quoted price for a project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example quoted price: programmer 280 hrs × $39 + administration 60 hrs × $80 + building 150 days × $2 + insurance $50 = $16,070. Compare actual costs after completion to adjust estimates/rates if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-project reconciliation and rate adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: At period end, compare estimated costs and application rates to actual costs for each cost pool and activity; if variances are significant or new fixed costs occur, adjust future estimates, create new cost pools, and change quoted prices accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example Project 1 net loss of $80 triggers review of estimates (programmer hours, manager hours, days active) and potential adjustment of application rates for future quotations.
